# Running Your Expo App on a Physical iPhone (No Paid Developer Account)

This guide walks you through every step of creating an Expo app on your Mac and running it on your physical iPhone — **without paying $99/year for an Apple Developer account**. The key is building *locally* (on your own Mac) rather than using Expo's cloud build service (EAS), which requires paid Apple credentials for device builds.

> **What you'll need:** A Mac, an iPhone, a USB cable (Lightning or USB-C depending on your iPhone), and an Apple ID (the free one you already use for iCloud / the App Store).

---

## Part 1: Install the Required Tools

You need four things installed on your Mac before you begin: **Homebrew**, **Node.js**, **Watchman**, and **Xcode**. If any of these are new to you, don't worry — just follow each step in order.

### 1.1 — Install Homebrew (a package manager for macOS)

Homebrew is a tool that lets you install developer software from the command line. Open **Terminal** (search for "Terminal" in Spotlight, or find it in Applications → Utilities) and paste this command, then press Enter:

```bash
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
```

It will ask for your Mac password (the one you use to log in). As you type, nothing will appear on screen — that's normal. Press Enter when done and follow any on-screen instructions. If Homebrew tells you to run additional commands to add it to your PATH, run those too.

### 1.2 — Install Node.js and Watchman

Still in Terminal, run:

```bash
brew install node
brew install watchman
```

**Node.js** is the engine that runs JavaScript outside of a web browser — it's what powers all of the Expo tooling. **Watchman** watches your files for changes so the app refreshes automatically while you develop.

Verify Node installed correctly:

```bash
node --version
```

You should see a version number like `v22.x.x`. Anything 22.11.0 or higher is fine.

### 1.3 — Install Xcode

Xcode is Apple's development environment. It's a large download (~12 GB), so start this early.

1. Open the **App Store** on your Mac.
2. Search for **Xcode** and click **Get / Install**.
3. Wait for the download and installation to finish. This can take 30+ minutes depending on your internet speed.
4. **Open Xcode once** after it installs. It will ask you to agree to a license and install additional components — say yes to everything.

#### Install the Xcode Command Line Tools

1. With Xcode open, go to the menu bar: **Xcode → Settings** (or **Preferences** on older macOS).
2. Click the **Locations** tab.
3. In the **Command Line Tools** dropdown, select the most recent version (it may already be selected). If it's blank, click it and choose the option that appears.

#### Install an iOS Simulator (optional but handy)

While you're in Xcode Settings, click the **Platforms** tab. If no iOS simulator is listed, click the **+** button at the bottom-left, choose **iOS**, and install it. This lets you test on a simulated iPhone on your Mac, which can be useful for quick checks.

### 1.4 — Install CocoaPods

CocoaPods is a dependency manager for iOS projects (similar to how `pip` works for Python). Run:

```bash
sudo gem install cocoapods
```

It will ask for your Mac password. This uses the Ruby that comes pre-installed on macOS.

---

## Part 2: Create Your Expo Project

### 2.1 — Create the project

In Terminal, navigate to wherever you want your project to live (your Desktop is fine for now) and create a new Expo app:

```bash
cd ~/Desktop
npx create-expo-app MyFirstApp
cd MyFirstApp
```

The first command (`npx create-expo-app MyFirstApp`) downloads a template and sets up a complete starter project in a folder called `MyFirstApp`. The `cd` command moves you into that folder.

### 2.2 — Install the development client library

This library turns your app into a "development build" — essentially your own custom version of the Expo Go playground, but with full native capabilities:

```bash
npx expo install expo-dev-client
```

### 2.3 — Open the project in VS Code

Since you already have VS Code, open the project:

```bash
code .
```

(The `.` means "the current folder.") You can browse and edit your app's source files here. The main file you'll edit is `app/(tabs)/index.tsx` or `App.js`, depending on the template.

---

## Part 3: Prepare Your iPhone

### 3.1 — Enable Developer Mode on your iPhone

If your iPhone runs **iOS 16 or later** (most modern iPhones), you need to turn on Developer Mode:

1. On your iPhone, go to **Settings → Privacy & Security**.
2. Scroll down and tap **Developer Mode**.
3. Toggle it **on**. Your iPhone will ask to restart — let it.
4. After the restart, it will ask you to confirm. Tap **Turn On** and enter your passcode.

> If you don't see the Developer Mode option, try connecting your iPhone to your Mac with a USB cable first, then check again.

### 3.2 — Connect your iPhone to your Mac

Plug your iPhone into your Mac using a USB cable. If a "Trust This Computer?" popup appears on your iPhone, tap **Trust** and enter your passcode.

---

## Part 4: Build and Run on Your iPhone

This is where the "build locally without EAS" approach comes in. Instead of using Expo's cloud servers (which require a paid Apple Developer account for physical-device builds), you compile the app right on your Mac using Xcode.

### 4.1 — Run the build command

In Terminal, make sure you're inside your project folder (`~/Desktop/MyFirstApp`), then run:

```bash
npx expo run:ios --device
```

Here's what this command does behind the scenes:

1. **Prebuild**: It generates a native iOS project (an `ios` folder) from your Expo configuration.
2. **Compile**: It uses Xcode (which you installed earlier) to compile that native project.
3. **Install**: It installs the compiled app onto the device you select.

When you run it, Terminal will show you a list of available devices (your plugged-in iPhone and any simulators). **Use the arrow keys to select your physical iPhone**, then press Enter.

### 4.2 — Sign the app with your free Apple ID

Since you don't have a paid developer account, Xcode needs to use your **free Apple ID** to sign the app. The first time you build, you'll likely be prompted for your Apple ID credentials in the terminal, or you may need to configure this in Xcode manually. Here's how to do it manually (you may need to do this if the automatic process fails):

1. Open the file `ios/MyFirstApp.xcworkspace` in Xcode (you can type `open ios/MyFirstApp.xcworkspace` in Terminal after the `ios` folder has been generated).
2. In the left sidebar, click the **top-level project name** (the blue icon at the very top).
3. Under **Signing & Capabilities**, check the box for **Automatically manage signing**.
4. In the **Team** dropdown, select your Apple ID. If it's not listed, click **Add an Account** and sign in with your Apple ID.
5. You may see a warning that the bundle identifier is already taken. If so, change the **Bundle Identifier** field to something unique — for example, `com.yourname.myfirstapp`.
6. Close Xcode and re-run `npx expo run:ios --device` from Terminal.

### 4.3 — Trust the developer certificate on your iPhone

The first time you install an app signed with a free Apple ID, your iPhone will refuse to open it until you manually trust the certificate:

1. On your iPhone, go to **Settings → General → VPN & Device Management** (on older iOS versions, this is called **Profiles & Device Management**).
2. Under the **Developer App** section, you'll see an entry with your Apple ID email.
3. Tap it, then tap **Trust "your-email@example.com"**.
4. Confirm by tapping **Trust**.

Now go back to your home screen and tap the app icon. It should launch.

### 4.4 — Wait for the first build

The very first build takes a while — often **5 to 15 minutes** — because it's compiling all the native code from scratch. You'll see lots of output scrolling in Terminal. As long as you don't see a red **error**, it's working. Be patient.

Once the build succeeds, the app will appear on your iPhone and the Metro bundler (the JavaScript development server) will start running in your Terminal.

---

## Part 5: Develop Your App

### 5.1 — The development workflow

After the initial build, you generally **do not need to rebuild** every time you change code. Here's the typical cycle:

1. Edit your JavaScript/TypeScript files in VS Code.
2. Save the file.
3. The app on your phone **updates automatically** within seconds (this is called "hot reloading" or "Fast Refresh").

If the development server isn't running (for example, you closed Terminal), you can restart it without rebuilding:

```bash
npx expo start
```

Then open the app on your iPhone — it will reconnect to the server.

### 5.2 — When you DO need to rebuild

You only need to run `npx expo run:ios --device` again if you:

- Add or remove a native library (e.g., camera, maps, push notifications).
- Change something in `app.json` / `app.config.js` that affects native configuration (app name, icon, permissions, etc.).

For day-to-day JavaScript/TypeScript work, just save and watch it refresh.

### 5.3 — Make sure your iPhone and Mac are on the same Wi-Fi

The development server sends your JavaScript code to your phone over the local network. If your phone and Mac aren't on the same Wi-Fi network, the app won't be able to load updates. Keep them on the same network while developing.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

**"Unable to install app" or signing errors**: Go back to Section 4.2 and make sure your Apple ID is set as the signing team in Xcode. Try changing the Bundle Identifier to something unique.

**App crashes immediately on launch**: You probably need to trust the developer certificate on your iPhone (Section 4.3).

**Free provisioning profile expires after 7 days**: Apple's free signing certificates are valid for only 7 days. After that, you just rebuild with `npx expo run:ios --device` and it will re-sign the app. Your code is not lost — it's only the certificate that expires. A paid ($99/year) developer account extends this to one year.

**"No development team" error in Xcode**: Open the `.xcworkspace` file in Xcode and add your Apple ID under Xcode → Settings → Accounts.

**Metro bundler can't connect to device**: Ensure your Mac and iPhone are on the same Wi-Fi network. Some university or corporate networks block device-to-device communication — try using a phone hotspot if needed.

**CocoaPods errors during build**: Try running `cd ios && pod install && cd ..` then rebuild.

---

## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Create a new project | `npx create-expo-app MyApp` |
| Install dev client | `npx expo install expo-dev-client` |
| Build & run on iPhone | `npx expo run:ios --device` |
| Start dev server (no rebuild) | `npx expo start` |
| Clean rebuild from scratch | `npx expo prebuild --clean` then `npx expo run:ios --device` |
